<reason>Both sides converged on irreversibility as the decisive test, which made the debate clean to judge. CON (A) built a more mechanistic comparative case: the ban supplies the order book that turns a domestic prototype into a production tool, while shipped foreign tools remain a maintained state dependent on consumables, engineers, and software; chip denial already exists as the precise instrument. PRO (B) answered directly and with good epistemic discipline (refusing to invent a year-count, catching CON's slide from "a few years" to "months", and landing "chip denial never enters a plant you already equipped"), but its core counter to CON's mechanism—that a fused state won't stay dependent "out of gratitude"—sidestepped CON's actual point that switching happens by absence of a substitute, which the ban itself creates. CON also handled PRO's contradiction question with a coherent today/tomorrow layering and a clean dilemma. PRO's irreversibility route stayed live, and its answers to pressure were honest, but CON did more weighing and made the reversible-versus-irreversible choice sharper. Clear but competitive edge to A.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>A's Rebuttal 1 turning PRO's "confession" ([B2.3]) against it—if a sanctioned foundry reaches near-leading-edge on stretched older tools, the chokepoint sits above where military AI lives—combined with the servicing-lever/chip-denial comparison ([A2.7]-[A2.8]); PRO's best counterpunch was [B4.1]-[B4.2] ("chip denial is a tap on inventory; equipment denial is a lock on the factory; servicing is a tutor, not a kill switch"), which CON then answered by specifying what servicing does not transfer.</best_rebuttal>
